paragraphs: BadPart investigates vulnerabilities in models that predict a numerical value at every image pixel. Examples include estimating depth from a single image and estimating motion between images. The paper focuses on black-box attacks, where an attacker queries a model without accessing its internal workings, and changes a localized image patch to disrupt its predictions.

The method organizes patch optimization around squares. It combines probabilistic square sampling with gradient estimates derived from model scores to search for effective changes. This design addresses the scaling difficulties of earlier black-box patch attacks and provides one framework for both depth and optical-flow estimation.

Across seven models covering those two tasks, BadPart exceeds three baseline methods in attack effectiveness and efficiency. Against Google's online portrait-depth service, it produces a 43.5% relative distance error using 50,000 queries. The tested state-of-the-art countermeasures also fail to defend effectively. These results expose weaknesses in the evaluated systems, including an online service, under query-based patch attacks.
icml-2024-badpart-unified-black-box-adve.tldr: BadPart efficiently finds adversarial image patches that disrupt depth and motion estimation through black-box model queries.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether an AI assistant can learn to recognize questions outside its knowledge and communicate that uncertainty in ordinary language. The motivation is factual error: a model can produce a fluent answer even when it lacks the knowledge needed to answer correctly. The authors investigate whether training can improve its decision to decline.

They construct an “I don't know” dataset tailored to a particular assistant. Questions are categorized according to whether that assistant knows their answers. The dataset includes examples for supervised fine-tuning and preference data, allowing the authors to investigate different alignment methods. Making the data model-specific ties the desired response to the capabilities of the assistant being trained.

In the reported experiments, alignment makes assistants more capable of refusing questions outside their knowledge scope and significantly improves truthfulness relative to the original assistants. The finding supports training an assistant's answering behavior around its own knowledge boundaries. It establishes improved recognition and expression of those boundaries in the experiments, rather than perfect awareness of everything the model knows.
icml-2024-can-ai-assistants-know-what-th.tldr: Training assistants on model-specific examples of what they do and do not know improves appropriate refusals and truthfulness.

paragraphs: The paper asks when observational records can reveal how a digital platform's algorithmic actions change user consumption. Platforms often choose actions using predictions learned from historical behavior, so their actions are connected to the behavior researchers want to explain. The authors identify assumptions that make the causal effect identifiable without requiring randomized platform actions.

Their central move is to model consumption as a process unfolding over time. The platform becomes a controller that repeatedly responds to a changing system. This perspective makes the repeated interaction itself useful for causal analysis. Under the paper's assumptions, variation in consumption originating outside that interaction, together with appropriately responsive algorithmic actions, is sufficient to identify the effect.

The authors supplement the identification results with analysis of estimators that work with finite datasets and with empirical investigations. The contribution is a route to causal estimation tailored to prediction-driven platforms, where repeated responses carry information that a static analysis may overlook. The result remains conditional on the stated identification assumptions; it does not make arbitrary observational platform data causally conclusive.
icml-2024-causal-inference-out-of-contro.tldr: Modeling repeated platform–user interactions yields sufficient conditions for identifying algorithmic effects on consumption without randomized actions.

paragraphs: This paper examines why kernel regression can fit training data very closely yet behave differently on new examples. Its analysis concerns the over-parameterized regime with a fixed input dimension. The organizing feature is the kernel's eigenspectrum: the pattern of eigenvalue sizes, particularly how quickly those sizes decrease.

The authors derive bounds on kernel-matrix condition numbers, which describe how unevenly scaled the matrices are. They use these results to strengthen test-error bounds that apply at finite sample sizes. For polynomial spectral decay, their analysis recovers an existing bound. For exponential decay, it supplies a new, nontrivial bound using random matrix theory and kernel-regression tools.

Within the analyzed setting, polynomial decay leads to good generalization despite noisy labels, described as tempered overfitting. Exponential decay leads to poor generalization, described as catastrophic overfitting. The results also connect to the existing characterization of benign overfitting for sub-polynomial decay. Together, these distinctions show why fitting noisy training data does not by itself determine predictive quality: the spectrum helps distinguish substantially different outcomes.
icml-2024-characterizing-overfitting-in-.tldr: New spectral bounds distinguish tempered and catastrophic overfitting in the paper's kernel-regression setting.

paragraphs: Chatbot Arena evaluates language models through people's preferences between pairs of responses. This addresses a challenge that capability measurements alone do not settle: whether users prefer the behavior a model produces. The open platform crowdsources comparisons from a diverse user base and uses those comparisons to evaluate and rank models.

The paper describes the platform and analyzes more than 240,000 votes collected over several months. It also explains the statistical methods used to turn comparisons into efficient and accurate evaluations. A central part of the analysis concerns the quality of the inputs to that process: whether user questions meaningfully distinguish models and whether crowd judgments agree with expert judgments.

The authors find that the questions are sufficiently diverse and discriminating, and that crowd votes agree well with expert ratings. These findings support the credibility of the platform's preference-based rankings. The contribution combines a public evaluation mechanism with evidence about its collected data, making human preference a practical basis for comparing assistants.
icml-2024-chatbot-arena-an-open-platform.tldr: Chatbot Arena uses crowdsourced pairwise comparisons and statistical analysis to rank language models by human preference.

paragraphs: CTAG turns a text description into sound by programming a virtual modular synthesizer. The motivation is editability: neural audio generators can translate language into audio, but their large internal representations make the result difficult to adjust directly. A synthesizer offers a compact set of controls that a sound designer can inspect and change.

The method repeatedly updates the synthesizer's 78 parameters to produce an audio rendering of the prompt. Those settings remain available for further tweaking after generation. The resulting sounds emphasize essential conceptual features over detailed acoustic imitation. The paper compares this abstraction to a simple visual sketch that conveys an idea without reproducing every detail.

The reported results show that CTAG's sounds are distinctive and perceived as artistic, while remaining similarly identifiable to sounds from recent neural synthesis models. This supports its role as a complementary creative tool. Its appeal combines recognizable text-driven generation with a sound-making representation that remains accessible to subsequent human editing.
icml-2024-creative-text-to-audio-generat.tldr: CTAG generates recognizable, artistic sounds from text by adjusting 78 synthesizer parameters that remain easy to inspect and edit.

paragraphs: The paper considers learning a task from a single expert demonstration when the true reward function is unavailable. This setting matters when collecting multiple demonstrations is expensive or impractical. With only one example trajectory, useful reward signals can be sparse, leaving the learner with little guidance about how to approach expert behavior.

Transition Discriminator-based Imitation Learning, or TDIL, creates a denser substitute reward that accounts for the environment's dynamics. It trains a discriminator to distinguish valid transitions from invalid ones and uses that information to compute rewards. The reward encourages movement toward states proximal to expert states, connecting progress toward the demonstration with transitions supported by the environment.

In experiments across five MuJoCo benchmarks and the Adroit Door robotic environment, TDIL outperforms existing imitation-learning approaches and reaches expert-level performance using a single demonstration. These results support dynamics-aware proximity as a useful source of learning guidance. The contribution is a way to extract more actionable reward information from a scarce expert example.
icml-2024-expert-proximity-as-surrogate-.tldr: TDIL uses environment-aware proximity to expert states to provide denser rewards for learning from one demonstration.

paragraphs: GaussianPro addresses a weakness in 3D Gaussian Splatting: its dependence on the initial point cloud used to reconstruct a scene. Structure-from-Motion techniques can provide too few points on surfaces with little texture, especially in large scenes. That sparse starting representation makes optimization harder and can reduce the quality of rendered images.

The method progressively guides where additional 3D Gaussians should be created. Drawing inspiration from multi-view stereo, it uses already reconstructed scene geometry and patch matching to place and orient new Gaussians accurately. This gives the expansion process geometric guidance beyond the simple splitting and cloning strategies used in the original method.

Experiments on both large and small scenes support the approach. On the Waymo dataset, GaussianPro improves PSNR by 1.15 dB over 3D Gaussian Splatting. The result indicates that better-guided scene densification can improve rendering quality when the initial reconstruction is inadequate. Its central contribution is to use existing geometry to help repair weaknesses in how the scene representation grows.
icml-2024-gaussianpro-3d-gaussian-splatt.tldr: GaussianPro improves Gaussian-splatting reconstruction by using existing geometry and patch matching to guide the creation of new Gaussians.

paragraphs: Learning several reinforcement-learning tasks together creates a resource-allocation problem when those tasks differ in difficulty. Easier tasks can dominate training and interfere with learning harder ones, producing negative transfer. Scheduled Multi-Task Training, or SMT, addresses this imbalance by giving challenging tasks greater priority during learning.

SMT uses a task-difficulty metric to update its priorities dynamically. That connects the allocation of training resources to how demanding the tasks are, instead of allowing simpler tasks to overshadow them. The algorithm also periodically reinitializes key network parameters. This reset mechanism is intended to reduce the tendency to favor simple tasks and improve adaptability across the task collection.

The paper reports significant performance improvements on challenging Meta-World benchmarks, validating the scheduling approach in those evaluations. The findings support treating the order and emphasis of training as part of the learning algorithm itself. SMT combines dynamic prioritization with parameter resets to address both resource imbalance and the simplicity bias that can develop during shared training.
icml-2024-hard-tasks-first-multi-task-re.tldr: SMT improves multi-task reinforcement learning by dynamically prioritizing difficult tasks and periodically resetting key network parameters.

paragraphs: A calibrated model assigns confidence levels that match how often its predictions are correct. Expected calibration error, or ECE, is a common way to measure departures from that relationship. However, ECE can be discontinuous: small changes in a predictor can cause abrupt changes in the metric. This paper investigates the nature and practical significance of that problem.

The authors completely characterize ECE's discontinuities for general probability measures on Polish spaces. They then use that characterization to design Logit-Smoothed ECE, or LS-ECE. The new metric is continuous and easy to estimate, providing a way to measure miscalibration without the same discontinuity issue.

Initial experiments compare ordinary binned ECE with LS-ECE on pretrained image classifiers. The two measurements track each other closely in those tests. This suggests that ECE's theoretical pathologies may be avoidable in practice, while leaving the conclusion appropriately preliminary. The paper therefore contributes both a mathematical account of ECE's weaknesses and an empirical check on how much those weaknesses affect observed evaluations.
icml-2024-how-flawed-is-ece-an-analysis-.tldr: The paper characterizes ECE's discontinuities and introduces a continuous alternative that closely tracks binned ECE in initial experiments.

paragraphs: Estimating a quantity often requires first estimating other, supporting quantities called nuisance parameters. Substituting those estimates into the final calculation can introduce plug-in bias. Existing correction methods rely on a target's influence function, and estimating several targets can require repeated, target-specific debiasing work. This creates analytical and computational burdens.

Kernel Debiased Plug-in Estimation, or KDPE, refines an initial estimate through regularized likelihood-maximization steps. It works within the targeted maximum likelihood framework and uses a nonparametric model built from a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The implementation avoids requiring a separate influence function for each target.

The theoretical result is simultaneous debiasing for all pathwise differentiable targets that meet the paper's regularity conditions. Thus, the coverage is broad but explicitly conditional on properties of the targets and model setting. The authors also establish computational tractability and provide numerical illustrations supporting the theory. The approach matters because one refinement procedure can serve many eligible target quantities, reducing the need for repeated custom corrections.
icml-2024-kernel-debiased-plug-in-estima.tldr: KDPE simultaneously debiases eligible target estimates under regularity conditions without requiring influence functions in its implementation.

paragraphs: Semi-implicit variational inference builds flexible approximate distributions through a hierarchy, but their densities are difficult to evaluate. Classical methods therefore use substitutes for the evidence lower bound that can introduce training bias. A score-matching alternative, SIVI-SM, makes its objective tractable through a minimax formulation, at the cost of an additional inner optimization.

Kernel SIVI removes that inner optimization by restricting it to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, where the authors derive an explicit solution. Substituting this solution leaves an outer objective based on kernel Stein discrepancy. The hierarchical distribution structure makes that objective computable with stochastic gradient descent.

The authors bound the variance of the Monte Carlo gradient estimates and use the bound to establish convergence guarantees. Experiments on synthetic distributions and real-data Bayesian inference tasks demonstrate effectiveness and efficiency. The contribution connects a more manageable optimization procedure with supporting theory: kernel structure resolves the inner problem directly while retaining a trainable discrepancy objective for the approximate distribution.
icml-2024-kernel-semi-implicit-variation.tldr: Kernel SIVI replaces an inner optimization with an explicit kernel-based solution and provides convergence guarantees for the resulting inference method.

paragraphs: The paper studies scientific assistance that requires reading long textbook chapters, a use case not fully captured by scientific problem-solving ability alone. TutorEval is an expert-written question-answering benchmark covering multiple STEM disciplines. It combines long source contexts with free-form answers to evaluate language models in a setting closer to textbook-based assistance.

The authors find that fine-tuning base models on existing dialogue datasets produces poor TutorEval performance. They respond by creating TutorChat, containing 80,000 long synthetic conversations about textbooks. They use it to fine-tune Llemma models with seven billion and 34 billion parameters, producing math-specialized tutors with context windows of 32,000 tokens.

The resulting models excel on TutorEval and also perform strongly on GSM8K and MATH. These findings support training that directly reflects the demands of lengthy textbook conversations. The work supplies both an evaluation target and training resources for that setting. Its models, datasets, and evaluations are publicly released, with the datasets built from open-source materials.
icml-2024-language-models-as-science-tut.tldr: TutorEval and TutorChat support evaluating and training language-model tutors that answer questions using long STEM textbook chapters.

paragraphs: The paper asks when historical data can improve an online bandit learner that repeatedly chooses among actions with uncertain rewards. Its key complication is distribution mismatch: the offline observations may come from different reward distributions than the online interaction. More historical information therefore does not automatically translate into better online decisions.

The authors establish an impossibility result when no informative upper bound on that mismatch is available. In that setting, no policy that acts without future information can outperform UCB, even with offline data. When a nontrivial bound is supplied, their MIN-UCB policy can improve on UCB by using historical data when it is informative and ignoring it otherwise.

MIN-UCB has tight regret bounds both for analyses that depend on the particular problem instance and for those that do not. Numerical experiments corroborate the theoretical results. The contribution identifies a condition under which biased historical evidence becomes useful, then supplies a policy that adjusts its reliance on that evidence rather than assuming it is always trustworthy.
icml-2024-leveraging-biased-information-.tldr: MIN-UCB improves online bandit learning with offline data when an informative bound on distribution mismatch is available.

paragraphs: Preference-based reinforcement learning learns a reward model from human feedback, reducing the need to manually specify rewards. This paper focuses on an overlooked part of that feedback: the relative strength of preferences. Knowing which behavior is preferred can leave useful information about how preferences compare underused.

Listwise Reward Estimation, or LiRE, organizes trajectories into a ranked list to incorporate this second-order preference information in an offline setting. The list can be constructed efficiently using the same three-way feedback format employed by traditional methods. This makes the organization of feedback central to the approach, without requiring a different feedback type.

The authors also introduce an offline preference-learning dataset designed to reveal the effect of the estimated rewards. On that dataset, LiRE outperforms state-of-the-art baselines even with modest feedback budgets and remains robust to variations in feedback quantity and noise. The results support extracting more information through relationships across a ranked collection of trajectories when learning a reward model from limited human judgments.
icml-2024-listwise-reward-estimation-for.tldr: LiRE uses ranked trajectory lists to capture relative preference strength and improve offline reward learning from limited feedback.

paragraphs: Pedestrian trajectory prediction uses observed movement to estimate where people will go next. Many existing methods assume that the observation sequence is complete, even though missing positions create uncertainty about past behavior. MS-TIP addresses this issue by combining the reconstruction of missing observations with prediction of future trajectories.

The method uses transformers with diagonally masked self-attention to fill gaps in the observed sequence. Multi-scale hypergraphs then model different kinds of interactions, allowing prediction to account for complex relationships among pedestrians. A scenic-attention component learns contextual information from the scene, so the model's input goes beyond movement coordinates alone.

MS-TIP also uses an intermediate control point and a refinement module to infer future paths. The authors report extensive experiments supporting accurate trajectory prediction. The contribution brings several sources of information into a coordinated approach: incomplete movement history, interactions at different scales, and scene context. Treating observation repair as part of the prediction problem directly addresses the completeness assumption highlighted by the paper.
icml-2024-ms-tip-imputation-aware-pedest.tldr: MS-TIP jointly fills missing pedestrian observations and predicts future paths using interaction modeling and scene context.

paragraphs: The paper addresses brain-network classification for neurodegenerative disease by considering both network structure and relationships among diagnostic groups. Cross-sectional analyses can treat those groups as independent, overlooking disease progression. Brain networks also contain connections between both similar and dissimilar nodes, making a single uniform way of combining neighboring information inadequate for the stated challenge.

Adaptive Graph diffusion network with Temporal regularization, or AGT, uses node-specific convolution to capture low-frequency patterns associated with homophily and high-frequency patterns associated with heterophily. It adapts the relevant range for each node. A temporal regularization term also considers relative distances between diagnostic groups in the learned representation to capture sequential variation.

The resulting model provides interpretations at both node and group levels. Evaluations on ADNI and PPMI support its superiority for the tested graph-classification tasks. The contribution is a representation that accommodates mixed network relationships while incorporating progression among diagnostic groups. This evidence concerns classification on those disease benchmarks, with progression represented through relationships between groups in latent space.
icml-2024-neurodegenerative-brain-networ.tldr: AGT improves brain-network classification by adapting graph processing to each node and modeling progression-related relationships among diagnostic groups.

paragraphs: Many physical equations describe a family of systems whose behavior changes with parameters, such as the Reynolds number in fluid mechanics. Design optimization and uncertainty quantification may require evaluating solutions at many parameter settings. Physics-informed neural networks offer surrogate solutions, but repeated, time-consuming training makes this use case challenging.

Parameterized Physics-informed Neural Networks, or P²INNs, extend the approach by explicitly encoding a latent representation of the equation parameters. This gives parameter dependence a dedicated role in the model's representation. The aim is to model solutions across the parameterized problem, addressing the repeated-training burden that motivates the work.

Extensive experiments on one- and two-dimensional parameterized PDE benchmarks show better accuracy and parameter efficiency than the evaluated baselines. The method also proves effective against known failure modes in those evaluations. These results support explicit parameter encoding as a useful design choice for physics-informed surrogates, particularly when the application requires solutions at numerous points in a parameter space.
icml-2024-parameterized-physics-informed.tldr: P²INNs explicitly encode equation parameters to improve accuracy and parameter efficiency when modeling families of PDE solutions.

paragraphs: PEAK tests hypotheses about the means of multiple data streams while allowing the analysis to stop at a data-dependent time. Its non-asymptotic guarantee controls false positives at the chosen alpha level across stopping times. This matters when evidence is inspected repeatedly and the decision to collect more data depends on what has already appeared.

The method builds on testing by betting, first introducing a single-stream betting scheme with guarantees for error control, power, and evidence growth. It then combines streams through averaged capital, avoiding wasteful union bounds. Under mild regularity conditions on stream sampling, PEAK has power one. It also reduces computational overhead for pure-exploration bandit applications.

Experiments use synthetic data and the real-world HeartSteps datasets. In the tested bandit problems, PEAK reduces samples before stopping by up to 85% relative to existing stopping rules. It also matches state-of-the-art sequential-test performance while improving computational complexity. These findings connect valid repeated inspection with potential savings in both data collection and computation.
icml-2024-peeking-with-peak-sequential-n.tldr: PEAK provides stopping-time-valid tests across multiple data streams, with reported reductions in sample use and computational complexity.

paragraphs: Prompting4Debugging examines whether safety mechanisms for text-to-image diffusion models hold up against varied problematic prompts. Such mechanisms include filtering inputs or outputs and fine-tuning away unwanted concepts or styles. The paper argues that their reliability needs testing beyond a limited collection of prompts already labeled safe.

The authors introduce P4D, an automated debugging and red-teaming tool that finds prompts capable of exposing weaknesses in deployed safety mechanisms. They use it to investigate Stable Diffusion models equipped with safeguards. The focus is evaluating the reliability of those defenses by searching for cases they fail to handle.

The reported results show that around half of the prompts in existing safe-prompting benchmarks can be manipulated to bypass many tested mechanisms, including concept removal, negative prompts, and safety guidance. That percentage concerns the evaluated benchmark prompts and their manipulated versions. The findings support the paper's warning that limited benchmark evaluations can create unwarranted confidence in the safety of image-generation systems.
icml-2024-prompting4debugging-red-teamin.tldr: P4D automatically discovers prompts that expose weaknesses in tested text-to-image safety mechanisms.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement-learning agents can reach a training plateau, particularly on complex tasks with sparse rewards. Continuing training may then produce little progress. RICE is a refinement scheme that uses explanation methods to identify critical states and changes where the agent begins its exploration.

The method constructs an initial-state distribution mixing the environment's default starting states with the critical states identified through explanations. Starting from this mixture encourages exploration from parts of the task considered important by the explanation process. Explanations therefore play an active role in training by influencing which situations the agent gets to explore from.

With the paper's design, the authors establish a tighter sub-optimality bound, providing theoretical support for the refinement scheme. Evaluations in popular reinforcement-learning environments and real-world applications show significant gains over existing refinement approaches. The findings support changing the distribution of exploration starting points as a way to address stalled learning. The theoretical claim concerns the sub-optimality bound; the practical performance improvements are established through the reported evaluations.
icml-2024-rice-breaking-through-the-trai.tldr: RICE uses explanations to select critical starting states, helping reinforcement-learning agents improve after training stalls.

paragraphs: Preference-based reinforcement learning uses human judgments to learn rewards, reducing the need to hand-design a reward function. Its reliability can suffer when feedback is noisy, especially if a method depends heavily on high-quality expert preferences. RIME addresses this problem by making reward learning more robust to imperfect judgments.

The algorithm uses a sample-selection discriminator that dynamically filters noise from the preference data. However, selection itself can make mistakes, and those mistakes can accumulate. RIME therefore includes a warm start for the reward model to counteract this error buildup. The warm start also helps bridge the performance gap between pre-training and online training.

Experiments on robotic manipulation and locomotion show that RIME significantly improves the robustness of a state-of-the-art preference-based reinforcement-learning method. The contribution couples noise filtering with a response to the filtering process's own errors. This matters because reliable learning requires more than rejecting suspicious feedback: the reward model also needs a sufficiently stable starting point for the transition into online learning.
icml-2024-rime-robust-preference-based-r.tldr: RIME combines dynamic preference filtering with a warm-started reward model to improve robustness to noisy human feedback.

paragraphs: SAFE-T addresses early-phase clinical trials that seek a suitable drug dose for later confirmatory studies. The paper highlights two concerns with standard procedures: participant benefit may not be optimized, and differences between participant subgroups may be overlooked. It also notes that common parametric modeling assumptions do not fit many novel drugs.

The procedure adaptively allocates doses using nonparametric, multi-output Gaussian process models of toxicity and efficacy together with Bayesian optimization. It aims to improve utility for heterogeneous participants while respecting safety constraints and working with small samples. The authors provide theoretical guarantees for satisfying those constraints and report accurate final dose recommendations.

Evaluation uses realistic synthetic scenarios, where SAFE-T generally outperforms comparable methods and maintains performance as sample sizes and subgroup distributions vary. The authors also extend it to a new adaptive setting. These results support its potential to improve dose-finding procedures, with the reported empirical evidence coming from synthetic scenarios. The contribution brings participant utility, subgroup differences, and constrained exploration into one adaptive framework.
icml-2024-safe-exploration-in-dose-findi.tldr: SAFE-T adaptively selects doses for heterogeneous participants with safety guarantees and promising results in realistic synthetic trials.

paragraphs: Wasserstein gradient flow describes how a probability distribution changes during optimization in Wasserstein space. Generative models can approximate this continuous process with discrete updates using the JKO scheme. However, previous approaches that parameterize a transport map for each update have training complexity that grows quadratically with the number of steps, limiting scalability.

Semi-dual JKO, or S-JKO, reformulates the update using an equivalence between a JKO step and unbalanced optimal transport. The resulting semi-dual formulation reduces training complexity from O(K²) to O(K), where K is the number of steps. This directly addresses how training cost grows as more updates are used.

The model substantially outperforms existing Wasserstein-gradient-flow generators in the reported evaluations. It achieves FID scores of 2.62 on CIFAR-10 and 6.42 on CelebA-HQ-256, results described as comparable to state-of-the-art image generators. The contribution combines a more scalable optimization formulation with strong empirical image-generation results, making this distribution-based modeling approach more competitive in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-scalable-wasserstein-gradient-.tldr: S-JKO reduces Wasserstein-gradient-flow training complexity from quadratic to linear in the number of steps while achieving strong image-generation results.

paragraphs: Neural classifiers can express more confidence than their accuracy warrants. Calibration aims to bring those quantities into agreement so that confidence better reflects the reliability of a prediction. This paper studies recalibration of a trained classifier, a problem commonly approached through calibration maps fitted using additional datasets.

Tilt and Average acts on the classifier's final layer by transforming its weights. The approach focuses on the angular geometry of that linear layer and adjusts the corresponding weights. This places the correction inside the part of the model that produces its final classification output, offering another mechanism for changing confidence behavior.

The authors validate the calibration effect both theoretically and empirically. They report that the approach can improve calibration performance in addition to existing calibration-map techniques. The contribution is therefore a geometric route to recalibration, supported by analysis and experiments. Its stated benefit concerns how well confidence aligns with accuracy, making the final layer's weight geometry a useful target for improving the reliability of reported confidence.
icml-2024-tilt-and-average-geometric-adj.tldr: Tilt and Average improves classifier calibration by adjusting the angular geometry of the final layer's weights.
